title: What to do in the garden in February
excerpt: "Frost on the seedheads, sharp secateurs and a list for the year. What to do this month, and what to leave until the weather turns."
body: |-
  There's a morning most Februaries when the frost gets onto everything you left standing. The Phlomis heads go white at the edges, the grasses stiffen, and every old flower stalk in the border looks like it's been drawn in pencil. It's the best the garden looks all winter. It's also the morning a lot of people decide it's time to tidy up.

  Hold on a little longer. February is the month for getting ready, not for rushing. There's plenty to do, but most of it happens at the potting bench, in the shed and on the back of an envelope, not in the border.

  ## Cutting back, and when

  If you left your seedheads and grasses up over winter, this is the question: when do they come down? We've written about why we leave them standing in [Why we leave the seedheads standing](#gw-link:why-we-leave-the-seedheads-standing). This is the other half.

  Don't go by the calendar. Go by the plants. Get down and look at the base of each clump. When you can see new green shoots pushing through, that's your sign. Until then, the old growth is doing a job: it shelters the crown from frost and wet, and the hollow stems are still full of overwintering insects.

  - Deciduous grasses, like Calamagrostis 'Karl Foerster' and Miscanthus: cut right down to a few centimetres once the new shoots show, and before they get tall enough to snip by accident
  - Evergreen grasses, like Stipa tenuissima and the sedges: don't cut them at all, just comb out the dead bits with your fingers (wear gloves)
  - Perennials: cut back to the fresh growth at the base, a clump at a time as each one wakes up

  In the north, a lot of this will wait until March, and that's fine. If the ground is frozen or sodden, stay off it. You'll do more damage to the soil with your boots than you'll ever do to the plants by leaving them.

  Cut once the green shows and you'll only have to do it once.

  ## Winter pruning, and what to leave alone

  A few things want pruning while they're still dormant, before the buds break.

  - Apples and pears: take out anything dead, damaged or crossing, and open up the middle so air and light can get in
  - Wisteria: the second of its two prunes, cutting last summer's shortened shoots back to two or three buds
  - Late-flowering clematis, the ones that bloom from midsummer on: cut them down to a strong pair of buds near the base

  Just as important is what you don't touch. Plums and cherries should wait until summer, when they're less likely to pick up silver leaf, a fungal disease that gets in through winter cuts. Spring-flowering shrubs like forsythia, and early clematis like Clematis montana, have already made this year's flower buds, so prune them after they've flowered. And leave the old flower heads on mophead hydrangeas until the hard frosts have passed. They're keeping the buds underneath warm.

  Prune a forsythia now and you'll have a very tidy shrub with no flowers on it.

  ## Sorting out the tools

  This is the job for a cold, wet afternoon, and February has plenty of those. Bring everything into the shed or the kitchen (if you're allowed) and go through it properly.

  - Clean off old sap and dried soil from blades, with wire wool for anything stubborn
  - Sharpen secateurs and loppers with a whetstone or a small file, following the angle that's already there
  - Put a drop of oil on every pivot and spring, and wipe a little over the blades to keep rust off
  - Run a file along the edge of your spade and hoe: a sharp spade does half the digging for you
  - Check the handles for splits while you're there

  A sharp blade makes a clean cut, and a clean cut heals faster. It's also far kinder to your wrists.

  Clean and sharpen your secateurs. You'll thank yourself in March.

  ## Planning the year

  February is when the garden is at its barest, which makes it the easiest time to see what's really there. Walk round with a notebook and a cup of tea and be honest with yourself.

  - What did well last year, and what struggled
  - What's in the wrong place: too much shade, too much wind, or simply too big for where it is
  - Where the gaps are, and what might fill them

  Deciduous shrubs and most perennials can be moved now while they're dormant, as long as the ground isn't frozen. Take a good root ball, water them in and they'll barely notice. If something's been sulking in the same spot for three years, it isn't going to cheer up on its own.

  Then do the ordering. Seeds, plants, anything you want to grow this year. The good varieties go early, and a list made in February is a lot calmer than one made in a garden centre car park in May.

  The best gardens are mostly decided in winter, at the kitchen table.

  ## The short version

  - Cut back grasses and perennials when you see new green at the base, not before
  - Prune apples, pears, wisteria and late clematis now
  - Leave plums, cherries and anything that flowers in spring
  - Clean, sharpen and oil every tool you own
  - Walk the garden, make a list, order early

  When the weather finally turns and the soil warms up, [Ten jobs for the first warm weekend](#gw-link:ten-jobs-for-the-first-warm-weekend) picks up where this leaves off.

  February is for getting ready. March is for getting on.

  So pick one or two of these and do them this weekend. The tools are a good start: they don't mind the rain. And if the notebook turns into more questions than answers, it might be worth a conversation.
